name: Helmeted Hornbill
threat: This glorious hornbill uplisted 3 levels from Near Threatened to Critically endangered in late 2015.

Its highly-prized casque is unique in that it is almost completely solid and rich in ivory - leading to excessive hunting in recent years which is set to increase, with China the largest consumer of the casque.
Logging and agricultural conversion is contributing to the ominous pressure of hunting, and restoration is complicated further by the hornbill's slow reproductive cycle.

name: Vaquita
threat: The greatest threat to the remaining vaquita is incidental death caused by fishing gear.
Vaquitas are known to die in gillnets set for sharks, rays, mackerels and chano, as well as in illegal and occasionally permitted gillnet sets for an endangered fish called Totoaba.
It is believed that about 30 vaquitas are lost to these threats each year.

name: Golden Lion Tamarin
threat: Once at a low of 150 in a key habitat, Golden Lion Tamarins suffer from a range of human influences.
Extensive programmes have had fair success in reversing the trend caused primarily by habitat loss but also logging, mining, poaching and animal trade.
De-forestation limits purported success of re-introduction initiatives. Just 8% of original forest habitat size remains, resulting in behavioural effects such as in-breeding.

name: Golden Poison Frog
threat: This vivid dart frog is the most poisonous species, but it finds itself under considerable threat.
Deforestation in the name of agricultural development, humans settling in the frog’s range, logging, and planting as well as spraying for crops have all had a combined effect.
Only one Snake predator is unaffected by its toxin and terrible taste, but this hasn't deterred international trade, though sparse

name: Forest Owlet
threat: The cute and petite Forest Owl suffers from a number of influences upon its small numbers.
Illegal deforestation and forest fires have a major impact, and encroachment from humans for various reasons is a consistent problem.
The species is low on the food chain with various predators adding to issues, as well as it being hunted for eggs and body parts which are used for items such as drums.

name: Kemp’s Ridley Turtle
threat: The smallest marine turtle has declined through food and egg exploitation but mainly, accidental capture through shrimp fishing.
Kemp’s Ridley nests are unfortunately easy for both direct predators and humans to find, making growth of the species sporadic at best.
Racoons, Skunks and Coyotes and a portfolio of sea and land-based species find the nests easy as easy prey.

statistics.title: Estimated nests found on Texas Coast

name: Scimitar Oryx
threat: The Scimitar Oryx has immensely charismatic horns which proved too valuable a-source not to be hunted to extinction in the wild.
Before this hunting almost saw off the species, climate change in its previous range dramatically affected numbers, when the range Sahara dried up.
Since European settlement within the Oryx's range, numbers have only declined further.

name: Fiji Crested Iguana
threat: Fiji is a fresh paradise for an array of natural wonders such as one of the only colour-morphing Iguanas, the Fiji Crested.

However, these forests have undergone consistent and intense degradation through burning, grazing, human settlement and tourism development meaning forestry and beach loss have cost the Iguana dearly.
Their small frame signals easy prey for beasts such as Black Rats and feral Cats, who also utilise Iguana eggs.

name: Knysna Seahorse
threat: Unlike many of the species in pieces, the Knysna Seahorse's endangerment is not linked to human activity.
This seahorse rather, resides in such a limited range that events occurring to these estuaries would be catastrophic for the seahorse.
Floods occur within some of the 3 estuaries – the Knysna, Swatvlei and Keurbooms – and mis-management continues these kind of occurrences could lead to total extinction.

name: Brazilian Armadillo
threat: The Three Banded Armadillo of Brazil is a hard nut to crack – with only Pumas and Jaguars powerful enough to be a predatory threat.
But this species finds itself vulnerable from the loss of habitat to allow space for livestock and hunting for food.
The armadillo was the mascot of the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, yet only 3% of its range lies within protected areas.

name: Pygmy 3-toed Sloth
threat: The Pygmy Three-toed Sloths are situated on a lone uninhabited, protected island of Panama.
However, the lack of residents on the island unfortunately doesn’t stop visitors and plans to develop tourism on the island causes problems for the Sloth's habitat.
This sloth has become something of a flagship species, resulting in interested humans visiting the island to capture them for captivity.

name: Kakapo
threat: The evolutionarily distinct Kakapo is one of the many flightless birds which evolved in isolation without predators in New Zealand.

The lack of defences meant that when humans arrived in the range 700 years ago, it was hunted to intensely small numbers followed by further decreases when pest control predators for other species were introduced in the late 1800s.
Looking extinction in the eyes, the Kakapo is a rare recent success story and numbers now continue to grow slowly through an extensive recovery program.

name: Long-beaked Echidna
threat: The Long-beaked Echidna is one of the longest serving species on Earth but its time may unfortunately finally be coming to an end.

It hunts using its spiky tongue to find and digest worms, but is itself on the receiving end of hunting, by humans for food. It has also suffered from habitat loss in ranges now densely populated by locals.
A further development in the form of a nickel mine is being planned in an area with a major population of the Echidna.

name: African Penguin
threat: Once in abundance, the African Penguin’s decline in the past century has occurred with velocity.
Climate change and pollution from events such as oil spills has had an effect, but depletion of eggs via over-collection and intense fishing in the area has also impacted their status.
One oil spill in June 2000 caused a wipeout of 40% of the entire species. If that proportion of loss were to happen to humans today, it would equate to 2.9 billion people.

statistics.title: Estimated Breeding Pairs in South Africa

name: Greek Red Damsel
threat: This long and vivid damselfly which bares likeness to the Large Red Damselfly, is restricted to very limited ranges.
This aspect puts the fly under threat as climate change can affect the already poorly managed brooks very easily, and expanding tourism increases the threat.
Water pollution and replacement by concrete have a huge impact on the fly’s habitat, while recent dry summers have at times dried out the brooks completely.

name: Sun Bear
threat: Sun Bears have a delightful necklace pattern accompanied by a long tongue but their existence may unfortunately be a lot shorter.
Hunting and deforestation impact to varying degrees depending on the range, with forest fires, developments and logging all contributing to lost habitat.
Hunting is actually illegal in all of the Bear’s range but unfortunately as is so often the case uncontrolled, where some areas have seen populations halve in over two decades.

name: Rainbow Parrotfish
threat: A gorgeous array of colours spreads over this large fish but it's this size which helps place it under threat of overfishing.
This fish coasts into shallow water which increases the risk of being caught by fisherman, but its habitat has also declined rapidly over the past 25 years.
The quality of conditions of habitat which remains – especially coral reefs – is also declining, which Parrotfish use for food and shelter.

name: Bactrian Camel
threat: With 25-30 Bactrian Camels to be lost per year if current trends continue, this special specimen has a grim-looking future.
Consistent hunting over the past 30 years has caused significant decline while predation from wolves in the range adds to the problems faced.
The Chinese range of camels is being mined along with other development work, while Mongolia will lose 84% of its current population by 2033.

name: Wallace’s Birdwing
threat: Named after Alfred R. Wallace, this butterfly's struggles would sadden the great naturalist.
Located mainly in the Maluku Islands, the lowland areas of forest where the Butterfly resides has been greatly reduced by logging. The deforestation continues today within commercial context.
Mosquitos in the area have also posed a problem indirectly – as they are fought off by insecticides which also affect this beautiful Birdwing.

name: Somali Ostrich
threat: The Somali Ostrich, only declared a unique species as recently as 2014, is another unfortunate victim of human influences.
With a variety of questionable purposes such as water containers, ornaments and protective religious symbols, their eggs are intensely exploited.
Direct hunting for food, sport, feather usage for leather and exhaustion through the chase all lead to a very grim future, while the usual case of habitat loss causes further issues.

name: Red Panda
threat: The Wonderfully playful Red Panda is under threat from the common combination of habitat loss and to a lesser extent, poaching.
Human numbers in the Panda’s range doubled towards the end of the last Century with previous habitat being turned into housing, farmland and other developments.
Human hunting is invariably accidental, though in places the fur is used for caps and other apparel, whilst inbreeding depression adds another threat.

name: Malayan Tapir
threat: This interesting snouty specimen is yet another unfortunate victim of deforestation and hunting.

Much of the range is uncontrolled, allowing illegal logging to continue, and in Sumatra – its stronghold range – it suffers similar issues to other Sumatra-based species from consistent, relentless loss of forestry.
Hunting pressure has increased by the decline of other hunted species within the range still left, though is currently a secondary threat.

name: Diademed Sifaka
threat: This critically endangered Sifaka is under threat from hunting for food, but also primarily loss of the rain forest in its range.
Despite in theory providing protection, national parks are away from governmental areas meaning that encroaching within the range from local peoples is unmanaged.
When hunted, its fur is used for trade and the meat being used for food.

name: Iberian Lynx
threat: The Iberian Lynx is the world’s rarest cat species and could be the first to become extinct since the Sabre-toothed Tiger.

The Lynx’s story is tragic. Rabbits declined dramatically, taking away the most important food storage – Myxomotosis spread far and wide through France and Australia, introduced in 1952 by a French gardener attempting to control pests.
Little did they know the disastrous effect this would have on such a tremendous species.

name: Sumatran Rhino
threat: Once in abundance in Southeast Asia, the Sumatran Rhinoceros is now critically endangered with 50% per decade lost till the early 90s.
Rhinos’ body parts sell for various applications but a horn is worth around EUR 27,000, a major prize for poaching with uses including fabled poison protection.
Sumatra also has heavy deforestation occurring, but other aspects such as in-breeding depression look to have an even heavier price.

name: Chocoan Peccary
threat: A range of problems place this Peccary in danger, hunting being the most significant contributor.
In Argentina deforestation has soared with 33% lost in just 15 years, having a huge impact on Peccary who disappear without more than 87% of cover is left.
Rounding off these causes for concern is a mysterious disease which has troubled this species for decades.

name: Okapi
threat: This species which resemble a half-zebra, half-giraffe suffers from the usual combination of habitat loss and poaching.
Logging and human settlement within the previous range has impacted a steady decline since the mid 90s.
Complete protection in the Congo and the initiative Okapi Conservation Project symbolise the very real threat this species faces.

name: Javan Slow Loris
threat: Wide-eyed and little wonder as like other Loris species, it has been over-exploited by humans.
Easily captured through its slow movement, it is captured and used under the mythical pretence that it has healing or magical properties.
Also kept as an exotic pet, humans have also encroached upon the range and the species looks extinction in the eye.

name: Hirola
threat: This critically endangered antelope stares extinction in the eyes, and would be the first mammalian loss in Africa in modern history.
Predation, resource competition, poaching and diseases Rinderpest and Tuberculosis continue to decline numbers.
A sanctuary has recently been put in place with protection from outside influences and supplies a glimmer of light for Hirola's future.

name: Drill
threat: With a range of less than 220km2, this stocky primate is listed as highest priority African primate.
Human development within the range as well as general habitat loss mixed with illegal hunting has meant declining numbers for many decades.
The final 30th pieces is represented by a number of just 3,000 Drills believed to be left, with a highest estimate of 8,000.
